KEYWORDS
acute cholangitis, bile duct stent, biliary obstruction, emergency medicine, POCUS
1 CASE PRESENTATION
A 71-year-old female with Merkel cell carcinoma complicated by
metastatic biliary obstruction status-post common bile duct (CBD)
stenting 4 months ago presents with 2 weeks of epigastric pain and
chills. On examination, she is afebrile, tachycardic, hypertensive, and
has mild epigastric tenderness. Laboratory results are notable for elevated white blood cell count, lactate, and total bilirubin. Right upper
quadrant point-of-care (POC) ultrasound (Video 1) demonstrates a
dilated CBD to 1.6 cm with the presence of a stent within the lumen
(Figures 1 and 2). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography reveals
worsening intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary ductal dilation with
bile duct wall thickening and enhancement, worrisome for CBD stent
obstruction with developing infection. The patient received antibiotics
and fluids along with aggressive pain management. Gastroenterology
took the patient for urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stent exchange. The patient rapidly recovered and was
discharged 2 days later.
2 DIAGNOSIS: ACUTE CHOLANGITIS
Acute cholangitis is a clinical syndrome caused by biliary stasis and subsequent infection of the biliary tract. Acute cholangitis due to recurrent

biliary occlusion is a common complication of biliary stent placement,
with an estimated incidence of 36%.1 Diagnosis of acute cholangitis is
made based on evidence of systemic inflammation, biliary stasis, and
bile duct dilation or obstruction. POC ultrasound is reported to have
